beginner.whatItIs: The assault rifle you already own the moment you first load in. It fires single shots or short bursts, feeds 5.56x45mm, and costs nothing to buy back after a death.
beginner.whyItMatters: Free is the whole point. Everything you carry can be lost when you die, so starting from a rifle that costs zero to replace means a bad run sets you back only what you chose to add to it.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Use it while your bank is small, and keep it in mind afterwards as the rifle to drop back to on a run where you would rather risk nothing.

beginner.whatItIs: A 5.56x45mm rifle with a genuine full-auto setting at $1,200 a match, and the first assault rifle on the vendor screen that will accept attachments.
beginner.whyItMatters: The free starters are locked to single shots and short bursts and will not mount anything at all. This is where a rifle stops being a fixed object and becomes something you can put a sight and a grip on.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Buy it on your first trip to the vendor. Against the $10,000 a new account starts with, you can lose it several times over and still be kitting up.

beginner.whatItIs: A full-auto assault rifle in 5.45x39mm, and one of the cheapest rifles you can actually buy rather than start with.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the first step up from the free rifle into a weapon that will hold a trigger down, and it uses a calibre nothing else in your early kit competes for.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Buy it once you have enough banked that losing one kit will not stop you deploying again, and you want an answer at close range that the burst-only starter cannot give you.

beginner.whatItIs: A 5.56x45mm full-auto rifle behind two separate gates: Assault level 10, then a one-time $35,000 to unlock it, before you start paying $2,000 each time you take it out.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the first rifle that hands you a real magazine decision, a 35 round or a 50 round, so feeding the gun becomes part of building the loadout instead of something the gun decides for you.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Go for it once kills have carried your Assault track to 10 and $35,000 is money you can lose without stopping. Before that the same cash buys a great many matches with a rifle you already own.

beginner.whatItIs: A full-auto 5.56x45mm rifle at 2.92 kg, the lightest assault rifle the source documents, sitting behind Assault level 28 and a one-time $150,000 unlock, then $2,800 a match.
beginner.whyItMatters: The source publishes a weight for every weapon and every piece of armour and clearly treats it as a cost, even though it never spells out exactly what carrying more does to you. This rifle asks for less of that budget than anything else in its class.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Pick it when the rest of your kit is already heavy - high-tier armour, a launcher, a hammer - and you want the rifle to be the part of the loadout that is not the problem.

name: FAL
summary: Assault Rifle - caliber .308 Win, weight 4.25 kg, $6,000.

beginner.whatItIs: A full-auto rifle chambered in .308 Win, gated at Assault level 35 behind a one-time $250,000 unlock, and $6,000 each time you take it into a match.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the one .308 among the assault rifles, against the 5.56 that most rifles here use at 28 base damage. Season 02 trimmed .308 damage by 25%, but it still hits harder than 5.56. The cost is the ammunition, and .308 also waits longest for its armour-piercing variant, at WARDOG level 140. Those armour percentages come from player-collected testing rather than confirmed numbers, so treat them as a guide.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you can afford the rifle and the feeding of it - .308 runs $4 a round against 5.56's $1.50 - and you expect fights where landing one shot has to be worth something.
beginner.reliabilityNote: The source page these figures come from is labelled by the source itself as unverified, player-collected test data rather than confirmed or official numbers. Treat them as a starting point and expect them to move with the next patch.

beginner.whatItIs: A 5.56x45mm rifle firing single shots or short bursts, with no mounting points for attachments. The source publishes no price for it, and every number it does publish matches the free starter exactly.
beginner.whyItMatters: The source states that three free starting rifles share this caliber, and this is one of the three weapons that fit that description, so the useful question is not whether to buy it but which one your account happens to hand you.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Fight with it until the vendor is affordable, and let its complete lack of attachment points rather than its damage be the thing that tells you it is time to move on.

beginner.whatItIs: The third rifle sharing the free starter profile - 5.56x45mm, semi and burst only, 3.17 kg, no attachment mounts, and no price published anywhere by the source.
beginner.whyItMatters: Burst fire is a real limit in a game that drops a hundred players around one moving circle, because you do not get to choose the range you fight at. A fixed short burst is the same whether the target is across a field or already in the doorway.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Early, and deliberately at distance. The burst that fights you inside a building is closer to an advantage when you are picking at somebody a long way off.

beginner.whatItIs: A new Season 02 assault rifle in 7.62x39mm with a 28 round magazine. It costs $3,200 each time you take it into a match, behind Assault level 20 and a one-time $100,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: It puts a different round on the assault track, 7.62x39mm, which is shared just with the SKS. That round had its base damage cut by 19% in Season 02, so older figures you may have seen for it are out of date, and the source publishes no weight or fire rate for the rifle yet.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Consider it once Assault level 20 is behind you and $100,000 is money you can spare, and if you want a rifle on the SKS round rather than 5.56. Since its weight is unpublished, read the vendor screen in game before you build a loadout around it.

beginner.whatItIs: A 9x19mm pistol at $200 a match, opened at WARDOG level 18 for a one-time $15,000. It is the cheapest pistol on the list, and at 0.63 kg it ties the GGX 18 as the lightest.
beginner.whyItMatters: It costs so little that carrying one is effectively free, it feeds the cheapest ammunition in the game at $1 a round, and it takes a 33 round magazine or a 50 round drum, which is far more capacity than a sidearm normally offers.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Carry it once it is unlocked, more or less always. 9mm opens its flesh-damage round at WARDOG level 10, earlier than every calibre except 5.45x39mm, so it is one of the first guns whose ammunition you can upgrade.

beginner.whatItIs: A double-action pistol in .45 Colt, opened at WARDOG level 1 for a one-time $5,000 and then $250 every time you take it out.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the only weapon in the game chambered in .45 Colt. Every dollar you later spend on that caliber's ammunition upgrades applies to this pistol and to nothing else you will ever own.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Only if you want it for its own sake. A caliber with exactly one gun behind it is a poor place to put an ammunition unlock until you already know you like how the gun shoots.

beginner.whatItIs: A .45 ACP pistol at $300 a match, gated at WARDOG level 40, feeding either a 7 or a 10 round magazine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Its round is rated at 30 base damage against 9mm's 22 while costing the same $1, but it feeds a 7 or a 10 round magazine, so you get far fewer attempts than a submachine gun gives you. You are trading how many chances you get for what each one is worth.
beginner.whenToUseIt: As a sidearm for somebody who expects to draw it rarely and wants the few shots in it to count, not as the thing you plan to win a close-range fight with.

beginner.whatItIs: The full-auto version of the GGX 17: identical 9x19mm chambering, identical 0.63 kg, the same 33 round and 50 round magazines, with an automatic setting added. WARDOG level 85 and a one-time $125,000 unlock, then $1,000 a match.
beginner.whyItMatters: With the drum fitted this stops being a backup gun and becomes something closer to a very small automatic weapon that happens to live in the sidearm slot, without costing you any carry weight to do it.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When your primary is deliberately slow - a bolt-action, a launcher, a marksman rifle - and you want the close-range answer already on your body rather than back at the vendor.

beginner.whatItIs: A .50AE pistol holding 7 rounds, weighing 2 kg - about three times the GGX 17 - and unlocked at WARDOG level 65 for a one-time $75,000, then $750 a match.
beginner.whyItMatters: Its round is rated at 49 base damage, well above the 22 of 9mm and the 30 of .45 ACP, but .50AE costs $4 a round and does not open its flesh-damage variant until WARDOG level 95, which is late even measured against this gun's own gate.
beginner.whenToUseIt: This is a heavy sidearm for the later part of an account, not a first upgrade. Treat it as something you eventually earn rather than as a rung on anybody's progression.

beginner.whatItIs: A 9x19mm submachine gun at $1,375 and 1.4 kg, offered with four different magazines - 15, 20, 30 and 50 rounds - behind Medic level 20 and a one-time $75,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: Apart from the M249 SAW, which lists five, no other weapon the source documents gives you four magazine sizes to choose between, and it is a full-auto primary on the medic track, so the same class that revives teammates can carry it.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you play medic and want a light, fast-firing gun to go with the job. It also feeds 9x19mm at a dollar a round, so running it does not quietly add to the bill for the gun.

beginner.whatItIs: A 9x19mm submachine gun at $1,200 a match, opened at Medic level 15 behind a one-time $50,000 unlock. It weighs 2.9 kg and takes 10, 30 or 50 round magazines.
beginner.whyItMatters: It sits between the MP5 at Medic level 4 and the AMP-9 at Medic level 20, so it is a mid-point on the medic track rather than a first or last gun. The gate is a class level, which money cannot move.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you are already playing medic, have reached level 15 and have $50,000 to spare. The MP5 before it and the free PP-19 Bizon fire the same 9mm round at a dollar a round, so the unlock is what you are paying to change guns.

beginner.whatItIs: A 9x19mm submachine gun at $1,800 a match, opened at Medic level 4 behind a one-time $25,000 unlock, rather than by fighting anybody.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the clearest illustration of how unlocks actually work here. The gun sits behind healing and reviving teammates, so a player who never touches a bandage does not reach it no matter how many kills they pile up.
beginner.whenToUseIt: It arrives on its own if you play medic at all, which is also the most repeatable way to earn in the game. If you specifically want this gun, the route to it is a first aid kit, not a rifle.

beginner.whatItIs: A .45 ACP submachine gun at $5,600 a match, opened at Medic level 35 behind a one-time $200,000 unlock, feeding 13, 30 or 40 round magazines.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the only automatic weapon in the game chambered in .45 ACP, a round rated at 30 base damage against 9mm's 22 for the same $1 a round. The heavier hit costs you nothing per trigger pull - you pay for it once, at the vendor.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Late in a medic run, when the 9mm guns have started to feel thin. Since the ammunition costs the same, there is no ongoing penalty for carrying it once the levels and the $200,000 unlock are paid.

beginner.whatItIs: A new Season 02 submachine gun in 9x19mm that is unlocked from the start of an account, at $1,000 each time you take it into a match. Its one listed magazine holds 53 rounds.
beginner.whyItMatters: There is no level or unlock bill in front of it, so the first money you spend goes on the gun and its ammunition. 9x19mm costs $1 a round, which keeps a long magazine like this cheap to feed.
beginner.whenToUseIt: A sensible pick for a new account that wants an automatic weapon for close fights without grinding a class track first. In open ground with long sightlines, a rifle is the better answer.

beginner.whatItIs: A break-action 12 gauge shotgun at $400 with a fixed internal magazine, so you reload it round by round instead of swapping a magazine in.
beginner.whyItMatters: 12 gauge is the one caliber that plays by different rules. Its buckshot is actually worse against armoured targets than plain rifle ammunition is, and it is the only caliber with a fourth ammunition type, a rifled slug, which behaves like a rifle round again.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Indoors and at arm's length, against people who have not spent money on armour yet. Against a geared target at any distance it is the wrong tool, and the reload will make sure you find out.

beginner.whatItIs: A semi-automatic 12 gauge shotgun at $1,200, opened at Support level 10, so it fires as fast as you can pull rather than one shell at a time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Semi-automatic fire is the entire difference in a shotgun. A miss with the break-action ends the exchange and hands the other player the fight; a miss with this one is just a miss.
beginner.whenToUseIt: In and around buildings, and on the defending side of a fight where people are coming to you. It turns up naturally if you spend your matches building and hauling supplies for the team.

beginner.whatItIs: A 5.56x45mm light machine gun fed by a 100 round belt, weighing 7.5 kg, at $3,200 a match and Support level 20 behind a one-time $150,000 unlock. A 200 round box and the usual STANAG magazines are also listed.
beginner.whyItMatters: A hundred rounds of the game's most common ammunition at $1.50 each lets you keep a piece of ground under fire without stopping to reload. It weighs 7.5 kg, against 2.92 kg to 3.95 kg for the rifles that share the round, so it takes a large share of what you can carry.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When your job is to hold ground rather than cross it. The weight and the reload are both arguments for setting up behind something solid and staying there.

beginner.whatItIs: A 7.62x54mmR light machine gun fed from a 100-round box, also 7.5 kg, at $4,100 a match and Support level 15 behind a one-time $100,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: Its round hits harder than the 5.56 belt gun's 28, even after Season 02 cut 7.62x54mmR base damage by 20%, but it runs $6 a round, so a full 100-round load costs $600 of ammunition before you have fired a shot. This is the weapon where the ammunition bill can outgrow the gun.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When the people you are shooting at are in serious armour, or the distances are long, and the match is going well enough that feeding it is not what ends your evening.

beginner.whatItIs: A new Season 02 light machine gun in .308 Win, fed from a 50 round box. It costs $7,250 each time you take it into a match, behind Support level 30 and a one-time $200,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: .308 Win costs $4 a round, so a full 50-round load is $200 of ammunition before you have fired a shot. The round also had its base damage cut by 25% in Season 02, so any older number you remember for it is out of date.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Bring it as a support gunner when you can afford to lose both the gun and the ammunition bill, and your job is to hold a position rather than cross the map. Until Support level 30 and the unlock are in reach, the cheaper machine guns do the same job.

beginner.whatItIs: A semi-automatic marksman rifle in 7.62x39mm at $2,400, with no level requirement on it whatsoever.
beginner.whyItMatters: It shares 7.62x39mm only with the TCX-SPR, and that caliber opens its armour-piercing round at WARDOG level 60 - the earliest in the game, and well ahead of 5.56 at 84. Armour-piercing is the only ammunition that keeps working against high-tier armour, so getting there early genuinely matters.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you want reach sooner than any class track will hand it to you. It is one of the few mid-priced weapons that asks for money and nothing else.

beginner.whatItIs: A semi-automatic marksman rifle in 7.62x54mmR at $4,800 a match, opened at Recon level 12 behind a one-time $50,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: That $50,000 one-time unlock buys a 7.62x54mmR round delivered semi-automatically from a 5 or 10 round magazine - reach and per-shot weight without cycling a bolt between shots. Season 02 cut that round's base damage by 20%.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Once $50,000 is genuinely spare. Until it is, the same money is a very long run of matches with a rifle you already have, and those matches are what raise the levels everything else is gated on.

name: BMR-308
summary: Marksman Rifle - caliber .308 Win, weight 3.9 kg, $6,250.

beginner.whatItIs: A semi-automatic marksman rifle in .308 Win at $6,250 a match, opened at Recon level 20 behind a one-time $125,000 unlock, sharing its 20 round magazine with the FAL.
beginner.whyItMatters: It fires .308 Win semi-automatically from a 3.9 kg frame, lighter than the FAL and the MK22, the other .308 weapons with a published weight. A light gun that still throws a full-power round is the reason to pick it.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you are spotting for a squad and want the option of taking the shot yourself. Recon levels come from marking targets for other people, so this rifle shows up as a reward for a job you were already doing.

beginner.whatItIs: A new Season 02 marksman rifle in .308 Win that takes 10, 20 or 30 round magazines. It costs $7,400 each time you take it into a match, behind Recon level 25 and a one-time $100,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: The choice of magazine is the point: a short 10 rounder keeps the load light, a 30 rounder keeps you shooting. It shares .308 Win with the FAL, the BMR-308, the MK22 and the Evo-3 Ultra, so it pays the same $4 a round and carries the same 25% base damage cut from Season 02.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Pick it once Recon level 25 is reached, after the SVD at 12 and the BMR-308 at 20, and when you want a marksman rifle that lets you pick the magazine to suit the job. At $7,400 a match, expect to lose it sometimes.

beginner.whatItIs: A sniper rifle at $1,200 and 2.95 kg. The source publishes no caliber and no fire mode for it, so those two facts are genuinely unpublished rather than left out of this page.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is the cheapest and much the lightest thing in the sniper rack - the next rifle up, the Mosin Nagant, is about a kilogram heavier and nearly four times the price - which makes it the long-range option a new account can most easily carry and replace.
beginner.whenToUseIt: As a first long-range weapon, with the caveat that you cannot plan an ammunition budget around it until the source says what it feeds. Read the vendor screen in game before you build a loadout on it.

beginner.whatItIs: A bolt-action rifle in 7.62x54mmR at $4,500 and 4.1 kg, and the only sniper rifle the source lists as accepting attachments.
beginner.whyItMatters: Bolt-action means one shot and then a manual cycle, so everything rests on the first round landing. In exchange it fires the same 7.62x54mmR round as the SVD and the PKM, and it is the only rifle in its rack you can put an optic on.
beginner.whenToUseIt: From a position you can hold and then leave. The cycle is long enough that a miss usually means being found, so it rewards waiting for a shot and punishes talking yourself into one.

beginner.whatItIs: A sniper rifle with a 10 round magazine, at 5.8 kg and $5,200, opened at Recon level 18 behind a one-time $100,000 unlock. The source publishes neither its caliber nor its fire mode.
beginner.whyItMatters: Ten rounds is as deep as any magazine in the sniper rack, matched by the AMR 50 and nothing else, so you get more attempts from one position than a bolt-action gives you.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you expect to take more than one or two shots from the same place and would rather cycle a magazine than work the bolt after every round. Until the source names what it feeds you cannot budget its ammunition, so read the vendor screen in game before you build a loadout on it.

name: MK22
summary: Sniper Rifle - caliber .308 Win, weight 6.3 kg, $6,400.

beginner.whatItIs: A sniper rifle in .308 Win with a 5 round magazine, at 6.3 kg and $6,400, opened at Recon level 30 behind a one-time $150,000 unlock.
beginner.whyItMatters: It brings the .308 round into the sniper rack rather than the marksman rack, and Season 02 cut that round's base damage by 25%. The five round magazine is a deliberate limit on how often you get to use it, so the gun is built around the assumption that you will not need many.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you have a position you trust and one target that actually matters. Between the level, the $6,400 and .308 running $4 a round, this is not a rifle to sweep a treeline with.

name: AMR 50
summary: Sniper Rifle - caliber .50 Cal, weight 12.5 kg, $14,800.

beginner.whatItIs: A .50 Cal anti-materiel rifle at 12.5 kg and $14,800 a match, opened at Recon level 35 behind a one-time $200,000 unlock - the heaviest and the most expensive weapon the source documents.
beginner.whyItMatters: Its ammunition is a category of its own: $50 a round, sold in boxes of five for $250. The source documents a single type for it, the standard round, and publishes no flesh or piercing variant - so there is nothing to upgrade into and nothing to save for.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Against vehicles and hard targets, from a spot you probably drove to. A full 10 round magazine is $500 before you have fired any of it, so every shot is a decision rather than an attempt.

name: Compound Bow
summary: Bow - ammunition Standard Arrows, weight 1.3 kg, $1,350.

beginner.whatItIs: A bow firing standard arrows at $1,350 a match and 1.3 kg, opened at Recon level 16 behind a one-time $150,000 unlock, with no caliber, no magazine and no ammunition tiers to buy into.
beginner.whyItMatters: Against armour an arrow is rated exactly like a rifled slug and like standard rifle ammunition, holding from 70% of its damage at the lowest armour tier down to 35% at the highest. Unlike every gun it starts at its ceiling and never improves. Those armour percentages come from player-collected testing rather than confirmed numbers, so treat them as a guide.
beginner.whenToUseIt: When you want a weapon whose running cost never changes. There are no better arrows waiting at a higher level, which makes it one of the few things in the game that is exactly as good at level 100 as it is on your first match.
beginner.reliabilityNote: The source page these figures come from is labelled by the source itself as unverified, player-collected test data rather than confirmed or official numbers. Treat them as a starting point and expect them to move with the next patch.
